newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government urged to help Washington.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government urged to help Washington.

text.p: The federal government will be asked Thursday to assume some responsibility for the severe problems that have led to the financial chaos, crumbling services and collapsing school system in the nation's capital.

The District of Columbia Control Board, ordered by Congress last year to take over running the near-bankrupt city, will release a strategic plan for Washington in which the U.S. government will be asked to help ease the financial burden, according to a draft obtained by Reuters Wednesday.
Among the programs slated by the board for possible federal funding were prisons, Medicaid, mental health care and maintenance of roads and bridges.
The five-member panel concluded that much of the District's financial strain was a product of its unique status, according to the draft.

The District is not a state but must provide the same services as one. It pays for such expensive items as its own prisons and medical care for the poor while other U.S. cities pass along these costs to their state governments.
For most of its history, the 10-mile-square enclave that came to be called the District of Columbia was controlled by the federal government and Congress.
However, in 1974 Congress relinquished that power, awarded the District home rule and the right to vote for a mayor and city council.

"The authority is convinced that one of the most basic reasons for the District's continued financial problems is that the capital is not supported -- as is every other city in the United States -- by a state," the Control Board said.
"The burden and costs that other states bear for their cities need to be borne for this city by the federal government," it concluded.

The board said it would recommend by March 31 options for a more equitable financial structure and would make specific recommendations by Sept. 30 for reorganizing the city's government and its delivery of services.

Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a troubled city of 570,000 people, many poor and black. The city is short of fire trucks and emergency vehicles; police cars go unrepaired, potholes unfilled; crime flourishes and a general had to be appointed by the control board to run its schools.
The District faces a budget shortfall of $85 million this year, which must be met through further aggressive cuts in city spending and personnel.
